title: Practice Exam 7
description: An additional full-length 36-question simulated California Class C knowledge exam. Challenging level.

questions.question: An ambulance approaches from behind with lights and siren while you are on a one-way street with parked cars on both sides. You should:
choices: Pull as far right as possible and stop, even on a one-way street
Stop in the middle of the lane
Speed up to the next intersection
Pull left, since it's a one-way street
questions.explanation: Pull toward the nearest edge (usually the right) and stop. On a one-way street, move to whichever side gives the emergency vehicle the clearest path.

questions.question: A police officer signals you to pull over. You should:
choices: Signal, slow down, and stop safely as far right as possible, then stay in the car
Stop immediately wherever you are, even in a lane
Continue to a destination of your choice
Speed up to find a police station
questions.explanation: Acknowledge by signaling, pull to the right at a safe spot, turn off the engine, and wait with hands visible. Stopping in a live lane is dangerous.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Being Stopped by Police

questions.question: Approaching a stopped Caltrans truck with flashing amber lights and no open lane to move into, you must:
choices: Slow to a safe and reasonable speed as you pass
Maintain your speed
Stop until it leaves
Pass only on the shoulder
questions.explanation: The Move Over law: change lanes away from the stopped vehicle if you can; if you can't, slow down. It covers maintenance vehicles, not just police and fire.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Move Over, Slow Down Law

questions.question: A yellow diamond sign shows a black arrow bending sharply at 90 degrees. This warns of:
choices: A sharp right-angle turn in the road ahead—slow well down
A gentle curve
A side road joining
A winding road with several curves
questions.explanation: A right-angle arrow means the road turns sharply ahead (more than a curve). Slow significantly before reaching it.

questions.question: A square sign with a black 'T' symbol warns that:
choices: The road you're on ends ahead at a T-intersection
A truck route begins
A toll booth is ahead
Two lanes merge
questions.explanation: A 'T' symbol warns that your road ends ahead and you must turn left or right onto a through road—be ready to yield and stop.

questions.question: A blue rectangular sign on the freeway most likely provides:
choices: Motorist services such as gas, food, or hospitals
A speed limit
A construction warning
A no-passing zone
questions.explanation: Blue guide signs indicate services (food, fuel, lodging, hospitals). Green signs give directions and distances; white signs are regulatory.

questions.question: A traffic signal shows a steady green ball with a separate red arrow for left turns. You may:
choices: Go straight or turn right on the green ball, but not turn left
Turn left because the ball is green
Do nothing until the arrow turns green
Turn left after stopping
questions.explanation: The red left arrow overrides the green ball for left turns. You may proceed straight or right on green, but must wait to turn left.

questions.question: You face a steady yellow light with plenty of room to stop comfortably. You should:
choices: Stop before the limit line
Continue through, since yellow means go fast
Stop in the crosswalk
Speed up to clear the intersection
questions.explanation: Yellow means the light is about to turn red—stop if you can do so safely. With room to stop, you must stop before the limit line.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Traffic Signal Lights

questions.question: A pedestrian-crossing signal shows a flashing upraised hand with a countdown of 5 seconds. As a pedestrian you should not start crossing, and as a driver you should:
choices: Still yield to anyone already lawfully in the crosswalk
Proceed immediately since the hand is up
Honk to clear the crosswalk
Turn through the crosswalk quickly
questions.explanation: The flashing hand tells pedestrians not to start, but those already crossing keep the right of way until they finish. Drivers must let them complete the crossing.

questions.question: You parallel parked uphill with a curb. To leave, you set the wheels straight and then notice your front wheels were turned away from the curb. That setting was correct for:
choices: Parking uphill with a curb
Parking downhill with a curb
Parking downhill with no curb
Level ground only
questions.explanation: Uphill with a curb: wheels turned away so a backward roll catches the curb. Downhill (with or without curb) and uphill with no curb: wheels toward the edge.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Parking on Hills

questions.question: It is illegal to park or stop:
choices: On a marked crosswalk or within an intersection
18 inches from the curb
In a metered space with time remaining
Facing the correct direction on a two-way street
questions.explanation: Never stop or park in a crosswalk, intersection, on a sidewalk, within 15 feet of a hydrant, or blocking a driveway.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Where You May Not Park

questions.question: Children are crossing at a school crosswalk and the crossing guard has stepped into the street. The guard lowers the sign and waves you on while children remain on the far sidewalk. You should:
choices: Proceed slowly as directed, staying alert for any child who steps off
Wait until every child has left the area
Ignore the guard and follow the signal
Accelerate to clear the zone
questions.explanation: Obey the crossing guard's directions. When waved on, proceed slowly and stay ready to stop—children near the curb can still move unexpectedly.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — School Crossing Guards

questions.question: Why is 25 mph (or lower) important in a school zone even though it 'feels' slow?
choices: Lower speed greatly shortens stopping distance and survival odds if a child is struck
It's only about avoiding a ticket
Children can always be seen in time
Cars handle better at low speed
questions.explanation: A pedestrian hit at 25 mph is far more likely to survive than at 35–40 mph, and lower speed dramatically cuts stopping distance—crucial where children are unpredictable.

questions.question: Driving into a low, blinding sun, the safest actions include:
choices: Slowing down, using the sun visor and sunglasses, and increasing following distance
Speeding up to get past the glare
Using high beams to see better
Following the car ahead closely to use its shadow
questions.explanation: Glare hides hazards and brake lights. Slow down, use the visor and sunglasses, keep the windshield clean, and leave extra following room.

questions.question: On a road posted 40 mph, traffic is flowing at 30 because of rain. Driving 40 is:
choices: Unsafe and a Basic Speed Law violation given the conditions
Legal and expected, since the limit is 40
Required to keep traffic moving
Only risky at night
questions.explanation: When conditions and traffic call for a lower speed, driving the posted maximum can violate the Basic Speed Law. Match a safe speed for the rain and traffic.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Basic Speed Law

questions.question: The fastest you may drive in any alley, unless otherwise posted, is:
choices: 15 mph
20 mph
25 mph
10 mph
questions.explanation: Alleys carry a 15 mph limit. Drive slowly and watch for pedestrians and vehicles emerging from blind spots.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — 15 mph Speed Limits

questions.question: You're in a center two-way left-turn lane waiting to turn left, and an oncoming car is also in the same lane to turn left from the other direction. You should:
choices: Each may use the lane to turn, but you must not use it to pass and should turn only when clear
Race to turn before the other car
Treat it as a head-on travel lane
Stop and refuse to turn
questions.explanation: Both directions share the center left-turn lane to set up left turns. Don't use it to pass or travel; complete your turn only when oncoming traffic is clear.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Center Left-Turn Lanes

questions.question: Before drifting right to let a faster car pass on a two-lane road, you should:
choices: Check that the right edge and shoulder are clear of cyclists, pedestrians, or debris
Move right without looking
Brake hard to force them to pass
Speed up so they can't pass
questions.explanation: Easing right to be courteous is fine, but first make sure the edge is clear of cyclists, walkers, parked cars, or hazards. Never speed up when being passed.

questions.question: A dashed line separating a through lane from an exit-only lane means:
choices: You may move out of the exit-only lane while the line is dashed if you don't want to exit
You must exit
You may not change lanes there
The lane is for carpools
questions.explanation: A dashed line lets you leave an exit-only lane to stay on the freeway. Once the line becomes solid, you're committed; plan your move early.

questions.question: Reaching for a dropped item on the floor while driving is dangerous because it:
choices: Takes your eyes, a hand, and attention off driving—leave it until you can stop
Is only a minor manual distraction
Is safe at low speed
Improves your reaction time
questions.explanation: Reaching down combines visual, manual, and mental distraction. Leave the object where it is and retrieve it after you've safely stopped.

questions.question: A 16-year-old may use a wireless device while driving:
choices: Only to call 911 or report a genuine emergency
Hands-free for any purpose
For navigation apps only
For calls but not texts
questions.explanation: Drivers under 18 may not use any wireless device while driving except to summon emergency help. Even hands-free use is prohibited.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Teen Cell Phone Restrictions

questions.question: On a dry road at 50 mph, a safe following gap measured by the 3-second rule equals roughly:
choices: About 220 feet—the distance you travel in 3 seconds at that speed
Two car lengths
About 50 feet
One car length per 10 mph
questions.explanation: At ~50 mph you cover about 73 feet per second, so 3 seconds is roughly 220 feet. The time-based rule scales automatically with speed, unlike fixed car-lengths.

questions.question: You should add extra following distance specifically when:
choices: Visibility is poor, the road is slick, or a vehicle is tailgating you
Traffic is light and dry
You're driving downhill on a clear day
You're the lead car with no one ahead
questions.explanation: Stretch the gap to 4+ seconds in rain, fog, on slick roads, when towing, or when tailgated—any time stopping is harder or someone may rear-end you.

questions.question: If the car ahead suddenly stops and you rear-end it, the law generally treats the cause as:
choices: Following too closely—keeping enough distance is your responsibility
Always the front car's fault for stopping
A no-fault situation
The fault of road conditions
questions.explanation: A driver is expected to leave enough space to stop safely. Rear-end collisions are usually attributed to following too closely.

questions.question: A pedestrian in a wheelchair is crossing slowly in a marked crosswalk as your light turns green. You should:
choices: Remain stopped and let them cross completely before you go
Proceed because your light is green
Inch forward to encourage them
Turn around them quickly
questions.explanation: Yield to pedestrians, including those using wheelchairs, until they have completely cleared your path—your green light does not override their right of way.

questions.question: A bicyclist is riding in the same direction in a bike lane as you prepare to turn right across it. You should:
choices: Yield to the bicyclist, then merge into the bike lane within 200 feet of the corner to turn
Turn across the bike lane in front of the cyclist
Speed up to turn before the cyclist arrives
Honk so the cyclist stops
questions.explanation: Yield to the bicyclist first, then merge into the bike lane near the corner to make the turn from the curb—this avoids the 'right hook' crash.

questions.question: A pedestrian carrying a white cane has paused at the curb and pulled the cane back. This may mean:
choices: They are letting you proceed; move forward carefully and watch them
They will never cross, so ignore them
You must stop and wait indefinitely
They want you to honk
questions.explanation: A blind pedestrian who withdraws the cane and steps back is often signaling you to go. Proceed cautiously, but stay ready to stop if they move.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Pedestrians with Disabilities

questions.question: At a four-way stop, a car to your left and a car to your right both stopped before you. You proceed:
choices: After both of them, in the order they arrived
Before them, because you're between them
At the same time as the car on your right
Whenever you choose, since all are stopped
questions.explanation: First to stop, first to go. Cars that arrived before you proceed first, in arrival order; you wait your turn.

questions.question: You're on a through road and a car is stopped at a stop sign on a side street to your right. As you approach, the car begins to pull out. You should:
choices: Slow down and be ready to stop—even though you have the right of way
Maintain speed because you have the right of way
Speed up to pass before they enter
Swerve into the oncoming lane
questions.explanation: Right of way is something you give to avoid a crash. If another driver fails to yield, slow and be ready to stop rather than insisting on your right.

questions.question: Entering a roundabout, you should yield to:
choices: Traffic already circulating in the roundabout, from your left
Traffic waiting to enter behind you
No one, since roundabouts have no right-of-way rules
Only large vehicles
questions.explanation: Circulating traffic—which approaches from your left—has the right of way. Wait for a gap, then enter and proceed counterclockwise.

questions.question: Merging onto a freeway, the on-ramp lane you're in is about to end. You must:
choices: Complete the merge before the lane ends, yielding to freeway traffic
Stop where the lane ends and wait
Continue onto the shoulder
Force freeway traffic to move over
questions.explanation: Accelerate to traffic speed and merge into a gap before the ramp lane ends, yielding to vehicles already on the freeway. Don't stop on the ramp.

questions.question: On the freeway you realize you're in a carpool lane during restricted hours without enough passengers. You should:
choices: Wait for a broken (dashed) line, then merge out when safe
Cross the double lines immediately
Stop and wait in the lane
Exit by crossing all lanes at once
questions.explanation: Leave the HOV lane only where the line is broken, then merge across regular lanes one at a time. Crossing the double lines is illegal.

questions.question: Long freeway driving causes 'highway hypnosis.' To prevent it you should:
choices: Keep your eyes moving, scan mirrors and signs, and take regular breaks
Fix your gaze on the car ahead
Set cruise control and relax fully
Drive faster to stay engaged
questions.explanation: Staring straight ahead on a monotonous road dulls alertness. Keep your eyes scanning and stop for breaks every couple of hours.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Fatigue and Driving

questions.question: A friend who has been drinking insists they're 'fine to drive home.' The responsible action is to:
choices: Keep them from driving—take their keys, drive them, or arrange a ride
Let them drive, since they say they're fine
Have them drink coffee first, then drive
Follow behind them in case they need help
questions.explanation: An impaired person can't judge their own impairment. Prevent them from driving by taking the keys, driving them, or calling a ride.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Alcohol and Driving

questions.question: Which factor does NOT reduce the alcohol already in your bloodstream?
choices: Eating food or drinking coffee
Waiting an hour
Waiting two hours
The passage of time generally
questions.explanation: Only time lets your body metabolize alcohol. Food and coffee don't speed it up or lower your BAC—they may just mask how impaired you feel.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Alcohol and the Body

questions.question: A driver convicted of DUI with a passenger under 14 in the car faces:
choices: Additional, enhanced penalties beyond the standard DUI
The same penalty as any DUI
A reduced penalty for having a passenger
No extra consequence
questions.explanation: Driving under the influence with a child passenger adds child-endangerment enhancements on top of the DUI penalties.
